title: AI Engineer — Level 1: Foundations
description: Core concepts every AI engineer must answer without hesitation: transformers, embeddings, prompting, basic evaluation.

questions.prompt: In a transformer, what does the self-attention mechanism fundamentally compute?
options: A weighted mix of all token representations, where weights reflect how relevant each token is to the current one
A fixed positional ordering of the tokens in the sequence
The probability of the next token directly from the embedding table
A compression of the sequence into a single fixed-size vector
questions.answer_notes: Self-attention scores every token pair (via query·key dot products), softmaxes those scores, and uses them to build a weighted sum of value vectors. Each token's new representation is therefore a context-aware mixture of the whole sequence. Interviewers expect you to mention Q/K/V and the softmax over scaled dot products.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Definitional question asked at the start of almost every LLM interview.

options: A dense numeric vector representing the meaning of text, such that similar texts are close in vector space
A compressed ZIP of the text for cheaper storage
The tokenized form of the text as integer IDs
A hash that uniquely identifies the text
questions.answer_notes: Embeddings map text into a high-dimensional vector space where semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity (cosine similarity / dot product). They power search, RAG retrieval, clustering, deduplication, and recommendation. Token IDs are not embeddings — the embedding is the learned dense vector.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Foundational vocabulary; a wrong answer here ends the interview.

questions.prompt: What does the temperature parameter control during LLM sampling?
options: How much the next-token probability distribution is flattened or sharpened before sampling
The maximum number of tokens the model may generate
How much GPU memory the model can use
The size of the context window
questions.answer_notes: Logits are divided by the temperature before softmax. T→0 approaches greedy decoding (deterministic, picks the argmax); higher T flattens the distribution, increasing diversity and the risk of incoherence. Mention that T=0 is standard for extraction/structured tasks and higher T for creative tasks.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic sampling knowledge used daily when calling model APIs.

questions.prompt: Explain Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to an interviewer in under a minute: what it is, why it's used, and its main components.
questions.answer_notes: RAG grounds an LLM's answers in external knowledge: at query time you retrieve relevant documents (usually via embedding similarity search in a vector store), inject them into the prompt as context, and have the model answer from that context. Why: fresh/private knowledge without retraining, smaller hallucination risk, citable sources, cheaper than fine-tuning. Components: document ingestion + chunking, embedding model, vector database/index, retriever (often hybrid keyword+vector with re-ranking), and the generation prompt template. Bonus points: mention evaluation (groundedness, retrieval recall).
questions.difficulty_rationale: The single most common question in AI engineer screens since 2023.

questions.prompt: A model has a 200k-token context window. What does this limit?
options: The total tokens (input prompt + generated output) the model can attend over in one request
Only the length of the generated answer
The number of requests per minute you can send
The size of the training dataset
questions.answer_notes: The context window bounds everything the model attends to: system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results, and the tokens it generates. Practical consequences: prompt budgeting, truncation/summarization strategies for long conversations, and why RAG chunking matters.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic operational fact that shapes every application design.

questions.prompt: What is hallucination in LLMs, and name three practical mitigations you would apply in a production app.
questions.answer_notes: Hallucination = the model producing fluent but false or unsupported content, because it generates plausible token sequences rather than verified facts. Mitigations: (1) ground answers with RAG and instruct the model to answer only from provided context, saying 'I don't know' otherwise; (2) lower temperature and require citations to retrieved sources; (3) add verification layers — self-consistency checks, a second-pass judge model, or programmatic validation of extractable claims. Also: constrain output with schemas/tool calls where possible.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Standard screening question; the mitigations show production experience.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between pre-training and fine-tuning?
options: Pre-training learns general language ability from massive corpora; fine-tuning adapts that base model to a narrower task or behavior with far less data
Fine-tuning must always be done before pre-training
Pre-training uses labeled data; fine-tuning uses only unlabeled data
They are two names for the same process
questions.answer_notes: Pre-training is self-supervised next-token prediction over huge corpora, producing a general base model. Fine-tuning (SFT, and preference tuning like RLHF/DPO afterwards) adapts it with orders of magnitude less, usually labeled, data. Expect the follow-up: 'When would you fine-tune instead of prompt-engineer?' — answer: consistent style/format at scale, domain vocabulary, latency/cost via smaller specialized models.

questions.prompt: Why do LLMs use subword tokenization (e.g. BPE) instead of whole words or single characters?
options: It balances vocabulary size and sequence length while handling rare/unseen words gracefully
It guarantees every language uses exactly the same number of tokens
It encrypts the input for privacy
Whole-word tokenization is impossible to implement
questions.answer_notes: Character-level makes sequences very long (expensive attention); word-level explodes vocabulary and fails on unseen words. Subword schemes (BPE, WordPiece, unigram) keep vocabularies ~30k-200k, decompose rare words into known pieces, and keep sequences reasonably short. Practical relevance: costs are billed per token, and tokenization explains oddities like arithmetic and string-reversal weaknesses.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic but distinguishes people who understand the stack from API-only users.
